I'm in the process of formalizing the equalities of the alpha equivalences as shown in 'Alpha equivalence equalities'. I am currently at the point of having theorem 4.1 formalized which is the equality of our new (yet to be merged) named representation and a similar version using freshness instead of occurrence.

Now my question: Is anyone aware of similar papers showing equivalences of actual binding representations that would be worth a formalization? Preferably representations which are already established in CSLib.

So far the best match that I was able to find is 'Proof Pearl: de Bruijn Terms Really Do Work' (alternative open access) showing that de Bruijn is indeed equivalent to some alpha-quotiented lambda calculus. The paper already comes with a HOL4 formalization apparently.

Is there general interest in such equivalences? I've got the time, interest and university backing to invest some effort into such formalizations if of any use for anybody.

I in general would be interested in having proofs of such equivalences. You might be interested in this work I ran into a while back:

Chris Henson said in #CSLib > Named representation of lambda calculus:

...there is recent work on joint semantics of these different bindings: Categorical Foundations of First-Order Abstract Syntax. This is formalized in Rocq already, so there is something to closely reference if anyone is interested in this sort of work.

Indeed I already saw that one in previous discussions. Looks highly relevant and at the same time highly intimidating - I wouldn't really know where to start given my lack of category theory background, though I've started working through some introductory category theory texts recently. The existing Rocq formalization does ease the cost of entry somewhat, and I do know Rocq, so that's a plus. I would genuinely enjoy learning more about these topics in the process. I'll consult with my supervisor to see if this is a viable direction wrt time and long-term research goals.
Ah, sorry to repeat myself then. From my end, the categorical semantics approach is not a prerequisite to something interesting that could be in CSLib (in fact it presents some difficulties).
